explanation: Light takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, so radio talks with the Apollo astronauts had a pause of about 2.5 seconds between each question and its answer.

claims.text: In a vacuum, light travels 299,792,458 metres, about 300,000 km, in one second.
The average distance from Earth to the Moon is about 384,400 km.
Light takes about 1.3 seconds to travel from Earth to the Moon.
A radio signal's round trip between Earth and the Moon takes about 2.5 seconds, which caused a noticeable pause in conversations with Apollo astronauts on the Moon.

coldSolve.answerGiven: The distance from Earth to the Moon

evidence.restatement: Since 1983 the metre has been defined so that light in vacuum covers exactly 299,792,458 m each second, i.e. just under 300,000 km.

claimResults.note: The speed of light is an exact defined constant (SI), held in units.json as speed_of_light_ms; dividing by 1,000 gives 299,792.458 km, matching the label value 299,792 and the display 'about 300,000 km'.

evidence.restatement: The Moon's mean distance from Earth (centre to centre, the orbit's semi-major axis) is roughly 384,400 km, varying between about 363,000 km at perigee and 405,000 km at apogee.

claimResults.note: Standard reference figure. The key holds even at perigee (about 363,000 km), which is still longer than one light-second, so the comparison is safe under any measure of the Moon's distance. Separation is about 28%, ample.
Arithmetic on the two confirmed label values gives about 1.28 s, which 'about 1.3 seconds' states correctly.

evidence.restatement: Because a signal needed over a second each way, Houston's exchanges with the Apollo moonwalkers had a round-trip lag of roughly two and a half seconds that listeners could hear.

claimResults.note: Round-trip light time is about 2.56 s from the mean distance; 'about 2.5 seconds' is a fair round figure (it is the commonly quoted Apollo delay). The audible lag in Apollo lunar-surface communications is well documented.

issues.note: The exact round trip is about 2.56 s, so 'about 2.6 seconds' would be marginally more precise than 'about 2.5'. Not an error at 'about' precision.

coldSolve.answerGiven: The distance from Earth to the Moon

evidence.restatement: The speed of light in vacuum is defined as exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, so one second of travel is about 300 thousand km.

claimResults.note: Exact by SI definition. 'In a vacuum' is in the claim; in air it is a hair slower, still far under the Moon distance.

evidence.restatement: The mean centre-to-centre Earth-Moon distance is about 384,400 km; it swings between roughly 356,000 and 407,000 km over an orbit.

claimResults.note: Rival test: the closest perigee (~356,400 km) still exceeds 299,792 km, so the order holds at every point of the orbit and under both centre-to-centre and surface-to-surface readings (about 6,400+1,700 km less is still ~376,000). Displays 'about' so there is no precision problem.

evidence.restatement: Moonlight and radio take roughly 1.3 seconds to cover the 384,400 km to the Moon.

claimResults.note: 384,400 / 299,792 = 1.28 s. Matches the well-known 1.3 s figure.

evidence.restatement: A signal there and back takes around 2.5 seconds, which put a visible lag into Apollo voice exchanges between Houston and the Moon.

claimResults.note: Round trip 2.56 s. The claim is about the signal delay, which holds.

issues.note: The explanation says the pause between each question and its answer was about 2.5 seconds. That is the signal's minimum round trip; the real gap included the speaker's reaction time, so was a little longer. Harmless at 'about', but 'at least 2.5 seconds' would be tighter.

editor.reason: A and B pass; c1, c3 and c4 have calculation evidence in A, c2 confirmed directly by both (memo 18). Both wording notes on 'about 2.5 seconds' are within 'about'. Dedupe: p.sci.0207 shares the Earth-Moon distance as one side but tests the Sun's width, not the speed of light.
